questions.q: The definition of chronic kidney disease on this page describes the net consequence of a fall in viable nephrons. What intraglomerular hypertension ultimately results in?
questions.exp: Definition: net consequence of the ↓ in no. of viable nephrons leading to intraglomerular hypertension resulting in proteinuria. (Book p805)

questions.q: Fill up: GFR = viable no. of nephrons × single nephron (sn) ______.
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: GFR = viable no. of nephrons × single nephron (sn) GFR. (Book p805)

questions.q: Viable nephrons can be regenerated or replaced after birth.
opts: False — they are fixed according to birth weight
questions.exp: Viable nephrons: fixed according to birth weight; not regenerated/replaced. (Book p805)

questions.q: The number of viable nephrons in a person is fixed according to:
questions.exp: Viable nephrons: fixed according to birth weight; not regenerated/replaced. (Book p805)

questions.q: Match the following pathogenesis step to its consequence — 1) ↓ no. of nephrons  2) Glomerular hyperfiltration  3) Mechanical stretching … A) Intraglomerular hypertension  B) ↑↑ sn GFR to maintain GFR  C) Capillary, podocyte and mesangial cell injury
questions.exp: ↓ no. of nephrons → ↑↑ sn GFR to maintain GFR → glomerular hyperfiltration → intraglomerular hypertension → mechanical stretching of capillary, podocyte and mesangial cell. (Book p805)

questions.q: Match the following stretched glomerular cell to its response — 1) Capillary  2) Podocyte  3) Mesangial cell … A) Proliferation → glomerular sclerosis (GS)  B) ↓ nephrin expression via local RAAS activation through AT-II  C) ↑ capillary pore diameter → proteinuria (tubulotoxic)
questions.exp: Mechanical stretching: capillary → ↑ capillary pore diameter → proteinuria (tubulotoxic); podocyte → local RAAS activation via AT-II → ↓ nephrin expression; mesangial cell → proliferation → glomerular sclerosis (GS). (Book p805)

questions.q: All but one are components of the red-letter mnemonic written beneath the flowchart. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Mnemonic: IF TA GS — interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy, glomerular sclerosis. (Book p805)

questions.q: Fill up: Tubulotoxic proteinuria triggers interstitial inflammation, which releases ______ to drive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy.
questions.exp: Proteinuria is tubulotoxic → interstitial inflammation releases TGF-β → interstitial fibrosis (IF) + tubular atrophy (TA). (Book p805)

questions.q: The tubulointerstitium, the determinant of renal function decline, makes up what share of the kidney?
questions.exp: Determinant of renal function decline: tubulointerstitium (85-90% of kidney is tubulointerstitium). (Book p805)

questions.q: The tendency to progress independently of etiology sets in after what fraction of nephrons are destroyed?
questions.exp: Tendency to progress independent of etiology: after 50% nephrons are destroyed. (Book p805)

questions.q: A patient who has one kidney removed at birth retains fewer viable nephrons. To keep total GFR stable, each surviving nephron must:
questions.exp: ↓ no. of nephrons → ↑↑ sn GFR to maintain GFR (compensation of surviving nephrons). (Book p805)

questions.q: In the flowchart, the podocyte responds to mechanical stretching with local RAAS activation via AT-II.
opts: True, but only after 90% nephron loss
questions.exp: Podocyte → local RAAS activation via AT-II → ↓ nephrin expression. (Book p805)

questions.q: According to the page, the determinant of renal function decline in CKD is the:
questions.exp: Determinant of renal function decline: tubulointerstitium (85-90% of kidney is tubulointerstitium). (Book p805)

questions.q: In the CAUSES line at the foot of the page, the order of the entities after DKD is:
opts: CGN, then IN, then CTID, then ADPKD
IN, then CGN, then ADPKD, then CTID
CTID, then IN, then CGN, then ADPKD
ADPKD, then CTID, then IN, then CGN
questions.exp: CAUSES: Diabetic Kidney Disease (DKD) > Chronic Glomerulonephritis (CGN) > Ischemic nephropathy (IN) > Chronic TubuloIntersticial Disease (CTID) > Adult polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). (Book p805)

questions.q: In the same CAUSES line, DKD carries the label m/c and ______.
questions.exp: DKD: m/c worst prognosis; CGN: (and m/c). (Book p805)

questions.q: All but one appear in the CAUSES ranking line. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The line lists DKD > CGN > IN > CTID > ADPKD; Alport syndrome is not on this line. (Book p805)

questions.q: Match the following cause of CKD with its rate of fall of GFR (ml/min/year) — 1) DKD  2) CGN  3) IN  4) CTID … A) 4-6  B) 8-10  C) 2-4  D) 6-8
questions.exp: Table: rate of fall of GFR (ml/min/year) — DKD 8-10; CGN 6-8; IN 4-6; CTID 2-4. (Book p806)

questions.q: The rate of fall of GFR listed for diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is:
questions.exp: Table: DKD 8-10 ml/min/year. (Book p806)

questions.q: The rate of fall of GFR listed for ischemic nephropathy (IN) is:
questions.exp: Table: IN 4-6 ml/min/year. (Book p806)

questions.q: In the complications row of the causes table, which two columns carry the ↑↑ marks?
questions.exp: Complications row: DKD — ↑↑ vascular complications; IN — ↑↑ macrovascular complications; CGN and CTID are marked '-'. (Book p806)

questions.q: CGN shows ↑↑ macrovascular complications in the causes table.
opts: False — the CGN column is marked '-'; macrovascular is under IN
questions.exp: Complications row: CGN '-', IN ↑↑ macrovascular complications. (Book p806)

questions.q: A CKD patient with a long history of atheromatous vascular disease is losing GFR at about 5 ml/min/year. Which causes-column fits best?
questions.exp: IN column: rate 4-6 ml/min/year and ↑↑ macrovascular complications. (Book p806)

questions.q: The slowest rate of fall of GFR in the causes table, 2-4 ml/min/year, belongs to:
questions.exp: CTID: 2-4 ml/min/year. (Book p806)

questions.q: Match the following G stage with its GFR (ml/min) — 1) G1  2) G3a  3) G4  4) G5 … A) <15  B) ≥90  C) 15-29  D) 45-59
The GFR range for stage G2 is:
questions.exp: G2: 60-89 ml/min. (Book p806)

questions.q: The GFR range for stage G3b is:
questions.exp: G3b: 30-44 ml/min. (Book p806)

questions.q: Fill up: In the G table, stage G1 (GFR ≥90) qualifies only when ______ / biochemical / histological evidence is positive.
questions.exp: G1: ≥90 ml/min → radiological / biochemical / histological evidence (+). (Book p806)

questions.q: In the G table, stage G5 (GFR <15) is labelled as:
questions.exp: G5: <15 ml/min → ESRD (uremic phase); mx: dialysis. (Book p806)

questions.q: Match the following A stage with its urine albumin-creatinine ratio — 1) A1  2) A2  3) A3 … A) >300 mg/g — severely ↑↑  B) ≤30 mg/g — normal  C) 30-300 mg/g — moderately ↑
questions.exp: A - ACR: A1 ≤30 mg/g normal; A2 30-300 mg/g moderately ↑; A3 >300 mg/g severely ↑↑. (Book p806)

questions.q: The upper limit of the A2 albuminuria band is:
questions.exp: A2: 30-300 mg/g (moderately ↑). (Book p806)

questions.q: A3 corresponds to an ACR above 300 mg/g and is described as severely raised.
opts: True, but only with GFR below 15
questions.exp: A3: >300 mg/g — severely ↑↑. (Book p806)

questions.q: A CKD patient has a GFR of 22 ml/min and an ACR of 450 mg/g. The staging is:
questions.exp: G4 = 15-29 ml/min; A3 = >300 mg/g. (Book p806)

questions.q: The A category of the classification is built on which ratio (ACR)?
questions.exp: A - ACR (urine albumin creatine ratio) as printed on the page. (Book p806)

questions.q: Fill up: The complications of CKD are captured by the mnemonic A, B, C, D and ______, with a separate U-line for uremic symptoms.
questions.exp: COMPLICATIONS: mnemonic ABCDE (A anemia/acidosis/access, B BP/bone, C cardiac, D dry weight, E electrolyte) plus U uremic symptoms. (Book p806)

questions.q: Match the following complication letter to its content — 1) A  2) B  3) C  4) D … A) Dry weight  B) BP and bone mineral disease (renal osteodystrophy)  C) Cardiac — m/c cause of death  D) Anemia, acidosis and access for dialysis
questions.exp: ABCDE: A — anemia (unfit for transplant; ↓ GFR independently), metabolic acidosis (↓ cardiac function), access for dialysis; B — BP, bone mineral disease (renal osteodystrophy); C — cardiac (m/c cause of death); D — dry weight. (Book p806)

questions.q: Under A of the complications mnemonic, anemia is highlighted because it makes the patient:
questions.exp: A — anemia: unfit for transplant; ↓ GFR independently. (Book p806)

questions.q: In the same A-line, metabolic acidosis acts by:
questions.exp: A — acidosis (metabolic) → ↓ cardiac function. (Book p806)

questions.q: All but one sit under A of the ABCDE mnemonic. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: A covers anemia, metabolic acidosis and access for dialysis; bone mineral disease is under B. (Book p806)

questions.q: The cardiac (C) complication chain runs: left ventricular hypertrophy → ______.
opts: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
questions.exp: C — cardiac (m/c cause of death): LVH → heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. (Book p806)

questions.q: In the C-line, calcification is listed as a reason the patient becomes unfit for transplant.
opts: False — only anemia causes transplant unfitness
True, but only with GFR below 15
questions.exp: C — cardiac: LVH → HFpEF; calcification → unfit for transplant. (Book p806)

questions.q: Fill up: The E-line of the mnemonic covers the electrolytes Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻ and ______.
questions.exp: E — electrolyte (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁻, K⁺). (Book p806)

questions.q: The D-line of the complications mnemonic stands for:
questions.exp: D — dry weight. (Book p806)

questions.q: A CKD patient is admitted with dyspnea; the echocardiogram shows LVH with a preserved ejection fraction. Under which letter of the complications mnemonic is this recorded?
questions.exp: C — cardiac (m/c cause of death): LVH → heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. (Book p806)

questions.q: The U-line of the complications list names:
questions.exp: U — uremic symptoms. (Book p806)

questions.q: In the diagnosis block, which kidney morphology is listed for a CKD work-up?
questions.exp: Diagnosis: B/L contracted kidney. (Book p806)

questions.q: All but one are in the 'all of' set written for diabetic nephropathy. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Diabetic nephropathy — all of: proteinuria, edema, hypertension, retinopathy. (Book p806)

questions.q: Fill up: The diagnosis block closes with a biopsy line looking for IF, TA and ______.
questions.exp: Biopsy: IF/TA/GS. (Book p806)

questions.q: The five numbered reversible causes to address include obstruction and ______.
questions.exp: Address reversible causes: 1. obstruction; 2. drugs/toxins/alternate medicines; 3. uncontrolled hypertension; 4. ECF volume ↓; 5. hypercalcemia. (Book p806)

questions.q: Uncontrolled hypertension is numbered which item in the reversible-causes list?
questions.exp: Numbered list: 1 obstruction, 2 drugs/toxins/alternate medicines, 3 uncontrolled hypertension, 4 ECF volume ↓, 5 hypercalcemia. (Book p806)

questions.q: Match the following reversible cause to its detail — 1) ECF volume ↓  2) Hypercalcemia  3) Drugs … A) Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus + afferent arteriole vasoconstriction  B) Diuretic excess / ↓ albumin  C) Toxins and alternate medicines
questions.exp: Reversible causes: ECF volume ↓ d/t diuretic excess, ↓ albumin; hypercalcemia → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, afferent arteriole vasoconstriction; drugs/toxins/alternate medicines. (Book p806)

questions.q: A CKD patient on aggressive diuretics with hypoalbuminemia develops worsening renal function. The reversible mechanism named in the list is:
opts: ECF volume ↓ from diuretic excess and ↓ albumin
questions.exp: Reversible cause 4: ECF volume ↓ d/t diuretic excess / ↓ albumin. (Book p806)

questions.q: Hypercalcemia is listed as a reversible cause because it drives nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and afferent arteriole vasoconstriction.
opts: True, but only in dialysis patients
questions.exp: Reversible cause 5: hypercalcemia → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, afferent arteriole vasoconstriction. (Book p806)

questions.q: The protocol on this page begins with:
questions.exp: Protocol: confirm diagnosis of CKD. (Book p807)

questions.q: For a patient fit for transplant, the hurdle listed on the page is:
questions.exp: If patient fit for transplant: hurdles — vascular complications (medial calcifications) → ↓ chance of success. (Book p807)

questions.q: Vascular complications with medial calcifications improve the chance of a successful transplant.
opts: False — they are irrelevant to transplant
False — they lower the chance of success
questions.exp: Hurdles for transplant: vascular complications — medial calcifications → ↓ chance of success. (Book p807)

questions.q: The transplant-success ranking written on the page is:
questions.exp: Success: CGN, CTID > DKD, IN. (Book p807)

questions.q: A CKD patient with chronic glomerulonephritis is being compared with one with diabetic kidney disease for transplant. Per the page, the better expected transplant success belongs to:
questions.exp: Success: CGN, CTID > DKD, IN. (Book p807)

questions.q: The dialysis-mortality co-relation graph plots mortality rate against:
opts: Urine albumin excretion over the same period
Days after the start of dialysis
Serum creatinine at the same time point
The GFR measured at the time of admission
questions.exp: Graph: mortality rate* vs days after the start of dialysis (0-360). (Book p807)

questions.q: On that graph, the mortality-rate curves sit at their highest during which window?
questions.exp: Mortality rate peaks early (≈34% at day 15-50 in age >65; ≈22-23% all patients) and falls over the 360-day course. (Book p807)

questions.q: Which curve sits lowest on the dialysis-mortality graph throughout the 360 days?
questions.exp: The age <65 curve runs lowest (≈6-7% early, ≈2% by day 350); age >65 runs highest (≈34% early). (Book p807)

questions.q: If a patient is fit for dialysis, the definitive indication listed is:
questions.exp: Indications: uremic symptoms (definitive); volume, K⁺, acidosis (relative). (Book p807)

questions.q: All but one are the relative indications bracketed in red. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Relative indications: volume, K⁺, acidosis; uremic symptoms are the definitive indication. (Book p807)

questions.q: Fill up: To create access, the named vessel connection is an AV ______ (6 weeks to mature).
questions.exp: Create access: AV fistula (6 weeks to mature). (Book p807)

questions.q: The AV fistula needs how long to mature?
questions.exp: AV fistula: 6 weeks to mature. (Book p807)

questions.q: A CKD patient has volume overload and serum potassium 6.4 mmol/L but no uremic symptoms. These indications are classified as:
questions.exp: Indications: uremic symptoms (definitive); volume, K⁺, acidosis (relative). (Book p807)

questions.q: Uremic symptoms are listed as a relative indication for dialysis.
opts: True, but only after a week
False — uremic symptoms are the definitive indication
questions.exp: Uremic symptoms (definitive); volume, K⁺, acidosis (relative). (Book p807)

questions.q: The graph of variation of GFR with plasma concentration is divided into overt renal failure and the:
opts: Hyperfiltration plateau of the early phase
Zone of overfiltration and protein overload
questions.exp: Graph zones: overt renal failure (GFR <25%) and zone of compensation (adequate renal reserve). (Book p807)

questions.q: Curve A on that graph — creatinine, urea and uric acid — behaves how?
opts: Depends largely on GFR for excretion; inverse relation with GFR
Rises only in the late stage of CKD, like the B curve
Stays normal throughout CRF, like the sodium curve
Follows the uric acid curve in overt renal failure
questions.exp: A: creatinine, urea, uric acid — depend largely on GFR for excretion; inverse relation with GFR. (Book p807)

questions.q: The substances named under curve B are:
questions.exp: B: PO₄, uric acid, K, H — ↑ only in late stage of CKD. (Book p807)

questions.q: Curve B substances rise only in the late stage of CKD.
opts: False — they stay normal in CRF
questions.exp: B: PO₄, uric acid, K, H — ↑ only in late stage of CKD. (Book p807)

questions.q: The mechanism for curve B is that the tubules increase excretion as GFR declines by:
questions.exp: B: tubules increase excretion as GFR declines — either by secretion or decreased reabsorption. (Book p807)

questions.q: Curve C (sodium) is described as:
questions.exp: C: sodium — normal throughout CRF (chronic renal failure); rate of excretion of Na per surviving nephron increases. (Book p807)

questions.q: Match the following substance to its curve — 1) Creatinine  2) Phosphate  3) Sodium … A) Normal throughout CRF  B) Inverse relation with GFR  C) Rises only in late CKD
questions.exp: A: creatinine (inverse with GFR); B: phosphate (late CKD); C: sodium (normal throughout CRF). (Book p807)

questions.q: All but one rise only in the late stage of CKD per curve B. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: B (late CKD): PO₄, uric acid, K, H; creatinine belongs to curve A. (Book p807)

questions.q: A patient in the overt-renal-failure zone (GFR 10%) still excretes sodium normally. The graph explains this because:
opts: The proximal tubule reabsorbs less sodium
The rate of Na excretion per surviving nephron increases
questions.exp: C: rate of excretion of Na per surviving nephron increases → sodium normal throughout CRF. (Book p807)

questions.q: Under the treatment heading, the holistic approach to CKD is:
questions.exp: Treatment: KDIGO 23; holistic approach to CKD: first line. (Book p807)

questions.q: The lifestyle block recommends salt restriction of:
questions.exp: Lifestyle: healthy diet — salt restriction (2-3 g/day). (Book p807)

questions.q: Risk-factor reassessment in the lifestyle block is recommended every:
questions.exp: Lifestyle: risk factor reassessment (every 3-6 months). (Book p807)

questions.q: Match the following lifestyle item to its detail — 1) Diet  2) Tobacco  3) Weight … A) Stop use of products  B) Salt restriction 2-3 g/day  C) Management
questions.exp: Lifestyle: healthy diet (salt restriction 2-3 g/day); physical activity; stop use of tobacco products; weight management; risk factor reassessment every 3-6 months. (Book p807)

questions.q: First-line management of proteinuria is:
opts: ACE(-)/ARBs plus SGLT2 inhibitors (curb the fall in GFR)
Loop diuretics — for volume overload control
Calcium channel blockers — for BP control only
questions.exp: Manage proteinuria: 1st line — ACE(-)/ARBs, SGLT2 (curb ↓ in GFR). (Book p807)

questions.q: The second-line agent for proteinuria, written in red, is:
questions.exp: 2nd line: finerenone (nonsteroidal aldosterone antagonist). (Book p807)

questions.q: The BP target for CKD in the first-line table is:
questions.exp: BP control: <120/80 mmHg — 24-hr ambulatory monitoring. (Book p807)

questions.q: Fill up: BP control in the table uses ACE(-)/ARBs or ______, which must not be combined with ACE(-)/ARB.
questions.exp: BP control: ACE(-)/ARBs or aliskiren (do not combine with ACE(-)/ARB). (Book p807)

questions.q: All but one are listed for BP control in the first-line table. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: BP control: ACE(-)/ARBs or aliskiren; non-dihydropyridine CCBs. Finerenone is the 2nd-line proteinuria agent. (Book p807)

questions.q: For LDL control (<100 mg/dl), the statin-based therapy named is:
questions.exp: LDL control <100 mg/dl — statin based therapy: rosuvastatin 20 mg/kg. (Book p807)

questions.q: Match the following LDL target to its group — 1) CKD  2) Diabetic CKD  3) Diabetic CKD with previous cardiovascular event … A) 70 mg/dl  B) 100 mg/dl  C) 55 mg/dl
questions.exp: LDL targets: CKD 100 mg/dl; diabetic CKD 70 mg/dl; diabetic CKD with previous cardiovascular event 55 mg/dl. (Book p807)

questions.q: Which set lists the contraindications for ACE(-)s written on the page?
opts: Pregnancy, B/L or unilateral renal artery stenosis, Cr rise >30% or K+ >5.5 mg/dl after starting, hereditary angioedema
Pregnancy, GFR below 30 ml/min, uncontrolled diabetes, resistant hypertension
Unilateral renal vein thrombosis, hypokalemia, gout and hereditary angioedema
Pregnancy, bilateral pulmonary fibrosis, hyperkalemia before starting and asthma
questions.exp: C/I for ACE(-)s: pregnancy; B/L or unilateral renal artery stenosis; if s. Cr ↑ >30%, s. K+ ↑ >5.5 mg/dl after starting Rx; hereditary angioedema. (Book p807)

questions.q: An ACE inhibitor must be reviewed if, after starting, the serum creatinine rises by more than:
questions.exp: C/I if s. Cr ↑ >30% (or s. K+ ↑ >5.5 mg/dl) after starting Rx. (Book p807)

questions.q: Bilateral renal artery stenosis is listed as a contraindication for ACE(-)s.
opts: False — only unilateral stenosis is listed
False — stenosis is a relative indication
True, but only in diabetic patients
questions.exp: C/I for ACE(-)s includes B/L or unilateral renal artery stenosis. (Book p807)

questions.q: A CKD patient with type 2 diabetes and a previous myocardial infarction needs an LDL target. The target is:
questions.exp: LDL targets: diabetic CKD with previous cardiovascular event — 55 mg/dl. (Book p807)

questions.q: SGLT2 inhibitors are included in first-line proteinuria management and they curb the fall in GFR.
questions.exp: 1st line: ACE(-)/ARBs, SGLT2 (curb ↓ in GFR). (Book p807)

units.title: Definition, pathogenesis flowchart and the causes line
units.guide: CKD is the net consequence of ↓ viable nephrons (fixed at birth weight, never replaced) → intraglomerular hypertension → proteinuria. GFR = viable nephrons × sn GFR: ↓ nephron number → ↑↑ sn GFR → hyperfiltration → intraglomerular hypertension → mechanical stretching — capillary (↑ pore diameter, tubulotoxic proteinuria), podocyte (local RAAS via AT-II, ↓ nephrin), mesangial cell (proliferation → GS). Mnemonic IF TA GS; TGF-β from interstitial inflammation drives IF+TA; tubulointerstitium is 85-90% of the kidney and the determinant of decline; progression becomes etiology-independent after 50% nephron loss. Causes line: DKD (m/c, worst prognosis) > CGN (and m/c) > IN > CTID > ADPKD.

units.title: CKD causes table: DKD, CGN, IN, CTID
units.guide: Rate of fall of GFR (ml/min/year): DKD 8-10, CGN 6-8, IN 4-6, CTID 2-4. Complications row: DKD ↑↑ vascular, IN ↑↑ macrovascular; CGN and CTID are '-'.

units.title: G and A classification (G1-G5, A1-A3)
units.guide: G table: G1 ≥90 (needs radiological/biochemical/histological evidence), G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15 = ESRD (uremic phase), mx dialysis. A table (ACR): A1 ≤30 normal, A2 30-300 moderately ↑, A3 >300 severely ↑↑.

units.title: Complications of CKD: the ABCDE mnemonic
units.guide: A — anemia (unfit for transplant, ↓ GFR independently), metabolic acidosis (↓ cardiac function), access for dialysis; B — BP, bone mineral disease (renal osteodystrophy); C — cardiac (m/c cause of death): LVH → HFpEF, calcification → unfit for transplant; D — dry weight; E — electrolyte (Ca²⁺, PO₄³⁺, K⁺); U — uremic symptoms.

units.title: Diagnosis and the five reversible causes
units.guide: Diagnosis: B/L contracted kidney; diabetic nephropathy = proteinuria, edema, hypertension, retinopathy (all of); biopsy looks for IF/TA/GS. Address reversible causes: 1 obstruction, 2 drugs/toxins/alternate medicines, 3 uncontrolled hypertension, 4 ECF volume ↓ (diuretic excess, ↓ albumin), 5 hypercalcemia (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, afferent arteriole vasoconstriction).

units.title: Protocol: transplant hurdles, mortality graph, dialysis indications and access
units.guide: Protocol starts with confirming CKD diagnosis. Transplant fit: hurdles = vascular complications (medial calcifications) → ↓ success; success ranking CGN, CTID > DKD, IN. Dialysis-mortality co-relation: mortality rate highest in the first 30 days (≈34% at day 15-50 in age >65, ≈22% all patients, ≈6-7% age <65) and falls over 360 days. Dialysis indications: uremic symptoms (definitive); volume, K⁺, acidosis (relative). Access: AV fistula, 6 weeks to mature.

units.title: Variation of GFR with plasma concentration (curves A, B, C)
units.guide: Two zones: overt renal failure (<25% GFR) and zone of compensation. Curve A — creatinine, urea, uric acid: depend largely on GFR, inverse relation. Curve B — PO₄, uric acid, K, H: rise only in late CKD via tubular secretion/decreased reabsorption. Curve C — sodium: normal throughout CRF because Na excretion per surviving nephron increases.

units.title: KDIGO 23 holistic approach: lifestyle, BP, proteinuria, LDL
units.guide: Holistic approach is first line. Lifestyle: salt 2-3 g/day, activity, stop tobacco, weight management, risk-factor reassessment every 3-6 months. First-line drugs: proteinuria — ACE(-)/ARBs + SGLT2i (curb ↓GFR), 2nd line finerenone (nonsteroidal aldosterone antagonist); BP <120/80 mmHg with 24-hr ambulatory monitoring, ACE(-)/ARB or aliskiren (never combined with ACE(-)/ARB), non-DHP CCB; LDL <100 mg/dl — rosuvastatin 20 mg/kg. LDL targets: CKD 100, diabetic CKD 70, diabetic CKD with prior CVD 55. ACE(-) C/I: pregnancy, B/L or unilateral RAS, Cr ↑>30% or K+ >5.5 after starting, hereditary angioedema.
